title: Jump Game IV
description: Find the minimum steps to reach the last index, moving to adjacent indices or teleporting between equal-valued indices, using BFS with one-time-use value groups.

blocks.text: Given an integer array arr, starting at index 0, in one step you may move to index i+1, index i-1 (both within bounds), or any index j where arr[i] == arr[j] and i != j. Return the minimum number of steps to reach the last index.

blocks.caption: BFS explores adjacent indices and same-value teleports, clearing each value group after its first use.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","arr[] (can contain duplicate values)"],["Moves","i+1, i-1 (within bounds), or any j with arr[j] == arr[i]"],["Start","Index 0"],["Goal","Minimum steps to reach index n - 1"]]}

blocks.text: Minimum steps in an unweighted move graph is BFS, but here each index also has "teleport" edges to every other index sharing its value. Grouping indices by value upfront turns "find same-value indices" into an O(1) map lookup, avoiding an O(n) rescan for every step.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The critical efficiency trick: once a value's entire teleport group has been used from ANY index sharing that value, it never needs to be considered again, since teleporting there again could never be faster.

Picture stepping stones in a row, each painted with a color (the array value). An explorer can step to an adjacent stone, or teleport instantly to any other stone of the SAME color. The question is the fewest moves to reach the last stone.

blocks.caption: A color's teleport group only needs to be used once across the whole search.

items: Teleporting to same-value indices is a single step, regardless of how far apart they are in the array.

Once a color's teleport group has been fully explored from the current BFS layer, that color is useless for any FUTURE index sharing it, since visiting it again could not be faster than the first exploration.
This is why the value-to-indices map should be cleared (or its entries removed) once a value group is processed, keeping the total work bounded.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Index 9 (the last index) is first reached at BFS layer 3, matching the expected output. The path uses two teleports (100 and 404) and one adjacent step.

A direct BFS treats every same-value index as a neighbor, looked up by scanning the whole array for matches on each visit. This is correct but can degrade to O(n^2) when many indices share the same value, since the same large group gets rescanned from multiple different starting indices.

Precomputing a value-to-indices map turns each lookup into O(1) group access. The key optimization: after processing a value's full group once, REMOVE that value from the map. Any later index with the same value will find nothing to expand through that value, since every reachable same-value index was already enqueued the first time that group was processed.
BFS using a precomputed value-to-indices map, but without clearing a value's group after it has been used once, so later indices sharing that value redundantly re-scan the (already-visited) group.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2) worst case","A value shared by O(n) indices can have its group rescanned from many different frontier indices"],["Space","O(n)","The value-to-indices map, visited array, and BFS queue"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Without removing a value's group after its first use, indices with a very common value can trigger the same large group scan repeatedly.

After processing a value's teleport group from any index, delete that value from the map entirely. Every index sharing that value that appears later in the BFS will find no teleport edges left to explore, since all reachable same-value indices were already enqueued the first time. This caps the total teleport-edge work at O(n) across the entire BFS.

items: BFS layer by layer; for the current index's value, if it still has a group in the map, enqueue all unvisited members, then delete that value from the map.
Also expand to i-1 and i+1 as usual adjacent moves.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, no group cleanup","O(n^2)","O(n)"],["Optimized, clear group after first use","O(n)","O(n)"]]}

items: Grouping items by a shared property (here, array value) upfront turns "find all related items" into O(1) map access instead of a rescan.
Once a group of "teleport" edges has been fully explored, removing it prevents the same large group from being redundantly rescanned by later visits.
This one-time-use-per-group technique is a general fix whenever a BFS/DFS graph has "hub" nodes connected to many others via a shared attribute.

blocks.text: Jump Game IV is solved with BFS over an implicit graph where each index connects to its immediate neighbors and every other index sharing its value. Precomputing a value-to-indices map and deleting each value's entry after its first use caps the total teleport-edge work at O(n), turning a potential O(n^2) rescan into a clean O(n) BFS.
